title: Western Ancestors, Part 3: Nyogen Senzaki
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells the story of Nyogen Senzaki, the Zen priest who arrived in San Francisco in 1905 with his teacher Soyen Shaku, drawing on Rick Fields' How the Swans Came to the Lake. Following the theme of effort, Nomon traces Senzaki from the Russell household, where Soyen Shaku leaves him in Golden Gate Park to face the city, through hotel work and a "floating zendo" of rented halls and borrowed chairs, to internment at Heart Mountain and a monthly bow across the ocean to Nakagawa Soen. Nomon asks what could sustain such steady, long-haul effort and leaves the question open. Nomon closes with Senzaki's recorded voice playing at his funeral and the first traditional seven-day sesshin in America, held in his memory.

sentences.text: Good morning, everybody.
It's wonderful that we get to be together.
So many friends from Seattle and Bellingham, both sanghas well represented.
Well, thanks, guy.
And friends from further away, Portland, California.
Old children of friends, grown-up children of friends.
So it just goes on.
Our theme being effort, I want to appreciate right away that we're all making an effort to be here.
More friends back there.
There were lots of other things we could have been doing today, and yet we made an effort to be here.
Whether we're staying for the day or the weekend or just the hour, we'll continue to make an effort, right?
The effort to be alive.
The effort to be ourself.
Or try not to be ourself, depending on what's going on.
The effort to help others.
The effort to continue.
Well, first I think we better acknowledge the difficult events in the world.
Another shooting.
Horrible.
When I was writing this, I almost wrote down "senseless shooting," because it certainly looks senseless from here, doesn't it?

An action that we can't really make any sense of: that a couple would stockpile weapons and make a plan to kill a bunch of people, coworkers, people on the street, people in a concert hall, people in a synagogue.
And probably it's only a matter of time before people in a zendo are shot.
It's a matter of time.
So it seems so senseless and horrible.
But we also know that people do things that make sense to them, that seem like the right thing to do in the moment or under the circumstances, given what they're thinking and feeling.
That's how people are.
Subjectively at least, except in some extreme cases of mental illness, or maybe we're all somewhat mentally ill anyway, everybody does what makes sense.
So somehow what happened in San Bernardino made sense to that couple.
But it doesn't make sense to us.
And maybe it's a blessing that it doesn't make sense to us.
It will never make sense to us, we hope.
But it's still horrible.
So many shootings, the world seems to be coming apart at the seams.
It's getting hard to keep track, right?
Was the last one Colorado Springs, or the other place in Colorado, the theater?
Or was it a college in Oregon, or an elementary school, a post office?
What a state of affairs.
And yet here's some interesting other news from the New York Times a little while ago.
A survey found that two-thirds of Americans believe that the portion of the world population living in extreme poverty has probably doubled in the last 20 years.
Another 29% of Americans in the survey believed that the proportion, sorry, of people in extreme poverty has remained basically the same.
So that's 95% of Americans who are completely wrong.
In fact, it turns out the proportion of the world's population living in extreme poverty hasn't doubled, and hasn't remained the same, in the last 20 years.
Actually, it's been reduced by half.
Depending on how you measure extreme poverty, it's either $1 a day or $1.25 a day, two different standards.
This article says that the percentage of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from about 35% of the world's population in 1993 to 14% in 2011.
So how does this affect the world when 95% of Americans are completely wrong about the way things are going in the world, at least in this particular way?
This is the journalist writing.
It was an op-ed piece.
The journalist writes that this also reflects a complete flaw in the way we journalists do our work: we only report on the disasters.
In 1990, more than 12 million children died before the age of five, and this toll has also dropped by half.
More kids than ever are becoming educated, especially girls.
In the 1980s, only half of girls in developing countries completed elementary school, and now 80% do.
So the most important thing going on in the world today is something that we never talk about, that we don't believe is happening: a rapid decline in poverty, illiteracy, and disease.
Granted that things are still pretty bad, he says. 16,000 children still die unnecessarily every day.
He writes, it's maddening in my travels to watch these children dying simply because they were born in the wrong place at the wrong time.
But, he says, one reason for our complacency about the world is the feeling that poverty is inevitable and getting worse, and that is simply not true.
The world's best kept secret, he says, is that we live at a historic moment, a historic inflection point when extreme poverty is retreating rapidly.
The United Nations recently put together a new plan that they hope will lead to essentially the complete elimination of extreme poverty by 2030.
The goals are historic, but current evidence suggests that this is actually possible.
This can be done.
And there have been recently some other statistics about safety, more directly relevant, I guess, to our school shooting horror.

Despite the horrible things that are going on in the world that we're aware of, the complete disaster of Syria (you can imagine living in one of those cities in Syria), the rise of ISIS, all these horrible shootings, still on the whole, much as the world is less impoverished than it ever has been, the world is safer than it ever has been.
Statistics suggest really strongly that this is the safest time in history.
You're the least likely to die young from violence or malnutrition or other things that are avoidable.
But it's funny, because it's really hard for our mind to think in terms of statistics and probabilities.
The concrete is what the mind holds so strongly.
And of course, statistics are no comfort to the families of the 14 people who died on Wednesday in San Bernardino, who just thought they were going to a work party.
But I think it's important to see if we can practice holding the horror in this broader reality: that actually there's less suffering, not more, overall, even if there's still far too much.
This doesn't make us complacent, it just spurs us on.
It makes us realize that what we do really matters, the efforts we make really matter, and we can be part of a solution.
Of course, then your mind's saying, well, what about global warming?
That's another talk.
I rode my bike today, anyway.
So anyway, I thought we can't just blithely talk about religion without recognizing the things that are happening, right?
So let's return to this theme of effort, which is, I suppose, a kind of effort: the effort to turn towards both the difficult things and the good things that are happening.
Effort's been very much in my mind and my attention these last weeks, because it takes a fair amount of effort to put on these retreats.
I want to especially thank people who put in a lot of effort, including everybody in this room, but especially Connie and Kate and Bob Rose, and probably other people who I should also name.
So thank you to all of you wonderful people for all your effort.
It's a lot of work to put on these retreats.
Even though we're reasonably skillful about how we organize it, of course there's always room for improvement.
We've done this a lot of times, and written descriptions of things and schedules and plans.
Still, it's not so easy, because the people who are doing the work, for good and ill, are people.
And people have all kinds of ways of going about effort, don't we?
Sometimes the effort of putting on retreats seems joyful and easy.
Other times it seems difficult and burdensome.
And it's really hard to tell why that is.
Are there particular tasks involved in putting on a retreat that are particularly difficult?
Are some of them easier than others?
Is it the task itself?
Is it the way we think about the task that makes it easy or difficult?
Is it the way we think about the near future, like, what's going to happen on Thursday night?
Are these people going to arrive?
Are we going to be ready?
It's a tricky thing, and the harder we think about it, the crazier we get.
And it's not right to just not worry about it either, right?
To just blow it off: oh, it'll work out.
They're all nice people.
They'll understand if we're not too organized.
That's not right either.
So how do you do it?
And what do we even mean when we say something's hard?
What does that actually mean?
It has a certain kind of weight in the mind.
Is it associated with some mental states?
Worry, anger, fear?
What does it mean when something's easy?

I was thinking a great advantage of sesshin, of sitting down and being quiet for a while, is that we can watch our mind, watch some of the patterns that are so automatic in us so much of the time when we're running around being busy.
We can start to discern a little bit: what is it about effort?
What is it in me that supports easeful effort, that supports angry effort, that supports fearful effort?
How does it feel in the body?
How does it go in the mind?
Is the hardness or the difficulty or the ease baked into the task and the situation?
Is it my fault?
Is it somebody else's fault?
Who knows?
I think it's a very complicated and interesting field of study for us, and very important to really reflect on what contributes when there's a flavor of suffering in our effort.
What is that?
The Buddha was quite clear about the root cause of suffering, wasn't he?
Grasping, he said, causes suffering.
Aversion causes suffering.
There are many different ways, small and large, subtle and blatant, that we want things to be a little different from the way they are.
We want ourselves to be a little different from the way we are.
And goodness knows, we sure want other people to be a little different from the way they are.
So the Buddha included the idea of right effort in his eightfold plan for working on this quality of suffering that we bring to our experience: right effort.
He gave many teachings on that, and then Buddhist practitioners, through the ages, have found ways to practice with this.
What's a sustainable effort?
And in Bellingham, we've particularly lately been thinking about how did this get here?
How did this happen, that we're sitting here in a Soto Zen zendo, some of us wearing Tang dynasty Chinese clothing, most of us having grown up in American suburbs?
How is this possible?

So we've been thinking particularly about the pioneering students and teachers who contributed to establishing this way of practice in America, in North America, in Bellingham, in Seattle, Canada, Mexico.
We've been exploring their stories, and in our practice period this winter, we're going to particularly explore some of their teachings.
Lately I've been thinking about one Zen priest who came to America very early in the 20th century, named Nyogen-Senzaki.
I want to read you his story, the story of a young Japanese man, Zen Buddhist priest and practitioner, who somehow ended up a part of our path and contributed in some way to this being here today.

When I was thinking about the effort of giving a talk, I realized that, yeah, for sure, the suffering involved in giving a talk, the kind that happens right before giving it, usually comes in the form of some kind of worry, right?
Are you going to say the right thing?
Is it the right topic?
Are you the right person?
Do you deserve to be in the seat, or whatever?
So I was just curious, what was my worry today?
My worry today is that the talk is going to be way too long.
I just want you to know that.
I don't know if that's true or not, because it's just a worry.
There's a little bit to the story of Nyogen-Senzaki, but I think it's worth spending some time on.
Nyogen-Senzaki came to America in 1905 with his teacher, So-yen Shaku, and we could do a whole talk on So-yen Shaku.
So-yen Shaku gave a Dharma talk at the World Parliament in religions in the 1880s, as far as we know the first Japanese or any Asian Zen school teacher to give a talk in America.
And 12 years later, he was invited to come back to America.
So-yen Shaku, the teacher of our focus this morning, wrote this poem on the boat.
*Like this boat on the spring ocean, a monk comes or goes by karma relations.
The horizon seems to be extending endlessly.
The current, however, takes us to the new world.
Yesterday the whales swam around us.
Today the clouds shut off sight of old Japan.
Following in the course of Bodhidharma from west to east I go.
And turning south I may visit India and Ceylon again, making the pilgrimage like Sudana.
Before long our boat will enter the Golden Gate.
And the seagulls perhaps will guide me to my destination.*
There's the Japanese priest on the boat in 1905.
He was a very innovative guy, So-yen Shaku.
Our historian believes he might have been one of the very, very few Japanese priests interested in the West.
He had also gone and practiced for a while with Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, which was very unusual.
Anyway, he was invited back to America by a couple who had met him when he was there in the 1880s, and who had come and visited him in Japan: Mr.
Alexander Russell of San Francisco.
*The Russells had visited So-yen Shaku at his temple in Gakuji during an around the world cruise they took.
He had permitted these Americans to join the monks in the training hall.
And from these Americans who ate barley gruel with the other monks and sat a full sesshin, So-yen had learned something about how to guide foreigners in Zen.
Because of this he was happy to accept the invitation from the Russells, which would provide him another opportunity to teach Zen to foreigners.*
*Mr.
Russell was a wealthy, civic-minded businessman with interests in mining, rubber, and real estate.
And Mrs.
Russell had traveled widely in the Orient where, she once told a reporter, she had studied all religions, taking what I think is best from each.
The Russells lived on the Great Coast Highway some miles from San Francisco with seven adopted children in the House of Silent Light, as Mrs.
Russell called the house, standing on a high bluff overlooking the Pacific surrounded by a wooden fence*
that sheltered a traditional Japanese garden from the wind.
Entrance was gained through a Japanese-style wicket gate.
And over the gate the Russells had hung a wood plaque carved with Soyen Shaku's calligraphy of the Chinese characters for silent light.
Soyen Shaku's room was specially furnished in Japanese style.
This is pretty unusual in 1905, even in California.
Mrs.
Russell had asked Soyen Shaku to teach her family Zen.
And during the nine months that he was their guest, he did just that.
"The daily life of this family is very religious," he wrote friends in Japan.

"Three times a day they practice Zen meditation, sing hymns, ring the handbell, have simple meals to the accompaniment of Western music, and the whole family, even servants, abstains from meat, wine, and smoking.
And they practice meditation every day."
And Mrs.
Russell became the first American to begin koan studies.
That's pretty interesting.
The first known Westerner, or at least known American, to do koan studies in Japanese Zen was Mrs.
Ida Russell of San Francisco in 1905.

Most of the Japanese Zen establishment, of course, thought this was impossible for Americans, and completely impossible for women, and therefore completely impossible for American women, to comprehend Japanese Zen.
But Soyen Shaku met their objections with a poem, which he addressed to Mrs.
Russell, alluding to the famous sixth Patriarch of Chinese Zen.
*The fifth Patriarch said, told his new monk, Southern monkeys have no Buddha nature.
That monk proved he had Buddha nature by becoming the sixth Patriarch.
In any part of the globe, where there is air, fire can burn.
Someday my teaching will surely go west, led by you.*
Soyen Shaku was joined at the Russells by a young student of his, a monk, named Nyogen Senzaki.
Senzaki's mother had been Japanese, his father Chinese, or Russian, we don't know.
He was born and immediately orphaned in Siberia, where a passing Japanese monk found him lying next to his mother's frozen body.
He was adopted by a shipwright named Senzaki, and then eventually came under the care of a Soto Zen priest and Buddhist scholar, who taught him Chinese classics and brought him up.
He was a very scholarly young man.
Supposedly by the time he was 18, he had read the whole Chinese canon of Buddhism, and had studied in Soto Zen and Shingon lineages.
And then eventually he hooked up with Soyen Shaku, the first teacher in our story.
Interestingly, the Japanese are so funny in some ways.
Apparently Soyen Shaku never told the Russells who Nyogen Senzaki was.
He just presented him as like a servant, like the house boy.
Didn't say he was an ordained Buddhist priest.
And Nyogen Senzaki lived in the servants' quarters at the Russells' and humbly helped out.
And Soyen Shaku went home after nine months, and Senzaki ended up, oh, excuse me, I'm telling the story out of order.
So about nine months into their stay, you see, I'm already realizing that everybody's just a touch, one moment.
So Senzaki in the house washed the dishes, did the laundry, cleaned the house, worked hard.
But as he remembered, he was a real greenhorn.
Although he knew enough English to read Carlisle's Sartor Resartus, which I don't know what that is, but it must be hard to read in English.
He could read that in his spare time, but he actually couldn't understand the spoken language at all.
And finally the housekeeper at the Russells' house decided she'd had enough of him.
So she sent Senzaki on his way with a five dollar gold piece.
So the relationship with this teacher remained obscure to the Americans.
And so that evening, Soyen Shaku accompanied Senzaki on his way to a Japanese hotel in San Francisco.
They were walking through Golden Gate Park when Soyen suddenly stopped, set down Senzaki's suitcase, which he had been carrying for his student, and said, "This may be far better for you.
Instead of being hampered by being my attendant monk, just face the great city and see whether it conquers you or you conquer it."
Then his teacher turned quickly away, said goodbye, and disappeared into the evening fog.
It was the last time Senzaki ever saw him.
So, classic Zen story.
Big teaching.
Which only would work if you were probably Japanese.
You know, we would be like, "Wait!
Hold on a minute here."
So there Senzaki is.
I mean, he was interested in America.
Deeply touched by Buddhism, right?
Kind of a prodigy young student.
But it said earlier that Nyogen Senzaki didn't really fit in with the Japanese Zen establishment either, so that was part of the reason he tagged along, probably.
In fact, he went off and tried to start a kindergarten because he felt little kids needed to understand something of the practice.
And kindergarten was a new idea from Germany he had just heard of.
But now here he is in America, trying to figure out what to do.
In 1910 Senzaki began in the hotel business.
He started as a porter, worked his way up to clerk, eventually manager.
He seemed to have gained this experience though without losing his innocence.
And he's not talking to anybody about Buddhism, it says in here too.
Just trying to figure out what to do in America.
For example, Senzaki could never understand why some customers would rent a room, stay in it for only a few hours, and then leave.
Why was that?
In 1916 he managed to buy a hotel with the help of a business partner.
Senzaki tried, but he was not a good businessman.
When the hotel lost enough money he gave it up.
Like, gave it up, you know, here.
And became the cook instead.
And at the same time he continued teaching Japanese and writing a little bit about Zen in Japanese newspapers.
One night in November 1919, so this is like what, yeah, 14 years since his teacher left, Senzaki woke from his sleep shivering with cold.
He lit a stick of incense and meditated until dawn.
Two days later a newspaper arrived from Japan.
Soyen Shaku had died at the age of 61 on that day.
And from that time he marked Soyen Shaku's death every year.
And then in 1922, 17 years after he'd arrived in America, he dared to, quote, "utter the B of Buddhism" to Americans.
He hired a hall with $20 that he'd saved up from working as a house boy and gave his first lecture.
In the lecture he translated a talk that Soyen Shaku had given earlier called "First Steps in Meditation."
But his English was so heavily accented that he had to write almost all the words down on a blackboard.
At the end of the lecture he asked people to leave their names and addresses.
From then on he would hire a hall whenever he had enough money.
Sometimes he would simply speak on Buddhism in a friend's parlor.
He called these various meeting places his floating zendo.
The only image present was a 600-year-old painting of Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, whose figure sits on the altar in Zen meditation halls.
He had it on loan from an art dealer.
In 1927, a brother monk by the name of Mayima visited San Francisco for three days.
When he returned to Japan, he helped out by raising $300 for the floating zendo.
Within a month, Senzaki had enough money to hire a hall and buy chairs for people to sit on.
He'd now established a zendo, one that he could carry as a silkworm hides himself in his cocoon, for 30 more years.
In 1931, Senzaki moved his floating zendo to Los Angeles.
The money for his move to Turner Street, where he held his meetings, came from the Japanese community.
Senzaki kept up the practice he'd started in San Francisco of instructing Japanese on one night and Americans on another.
Senzaki had followed Soyen Shaku's advice during his years in San Francisco.
He had met the challenge of the city head on.
He'd immersed himself in the world, even while he studied and practiced and prepared himself to teach Buddhism.
Now in Los Angeles, it was Senzaki the monk that appeared once again.
Having nothing in his possession, he had nothing to fear.
It was not easy to help Senzaki, since he would give everything away, anything he did not immediately need.
A favorite ploy among his students was to leave a $5 bill inside the meditation bell, hoping he wouldn't find it at first.
But when Senzaki did find it, he'd immediately invite the person who had left it to join him for dinner in a nearby cafe.
Senzaki didn't need much, but he knew how to enjoy himself.
The zendo in Los Angeles had two names, the Mentor Garden Meditation Hall, "mentor garden" like kindergarten, and Tozen Zenkutsu, meditation hall for the Eastern Dharma in Japanese.
He didn't try to teach his students the traditional cross-legged posture.
They sat in chairs for an hour's meditation once a week, heard a short lecture from Senzaki, chanted the four Bodhisattva vows, and left.
There was no socializing.
Everyone left in silence except for those who stayed behind to speak to Senzaki privately.
There was no statue of Buddha, just the painting.
Senzaki recited sutras three times a day, but "I do not mean to pray to this Bodhisattva," he reassured the students.
"A true Mahayana never worships anything but our true self.
The recitation is an expression of our wisdom and nothing else."
So he was doing this on his own, wasn't really interacting with the Japanese Buddhist establishment, which they didn't like too much, but it seemed natural enough to him in California.
He taught Zen because he felt it approached the true meaning of Buddhism most directly.
So he wasn't exactly sectarian either, trying to plant Zen.
He just thought Zen was a good path for the moment.
He remained removed from the sectarian squabbles that had become endemic among Japanese Buddhists.

Once a year, he led his students and friends on a Buddhist pilgrimage of Los Angeles, where by now, in 1938, there were Zen temples, a Shin temple, a Jodo temple, a Nichiren temple, and a Shingon temple, all serving the Japanese community of Los Angeles.
Which is an important side note: most of these histories written by convert Buddhists tend to focus on the interaction between convert Buddhists like us and Asian teachers.
Of course, there was also a lot going on in the Japanese immigrant community.
When Suzuki visited these temples, he visited each one, offered incense, and recited a poem.
Sometimes the priest also gave a short talk.
Suzuki's main supporter in Los Angeles was a Mrs.
Kin Tanahashi, proprietor of a Japanese bakery.
In the fall of 1934, Mrs.
Tanahashi was reading a Japanese magazine, Fujin Koran, in which she came across poems and diary entries from another young Japanese Zen monk named Nakagawa Soen.
Mrs.
Tanahashi showed Soen's work to Senzaki, and the two men began a correspondence.

Like Senzaki, Soen was disillusioned with the Japanese Zen establishment, and was living by himself on a mountain he called Daibosatsu Mountain, Great Bodhisattva Mountain, practicing zazen, eating wild plants, and making prostrations to the sun as it rose every day.
That was his practice, this other guy named Soen.
Senzaki had gone his own way in this strange land, as he called America, for 30 years when he began this correspondence with Nakagawa Soen.
But now at last, he had found someone who understood his rather unorthodox approach.
Perhaps this Soen would one day be able to continue his work.
Because remember, this was 30 years in, and Senzaki has like no students, exactly.
So Americans would come once a week, some friends in the Japanese community, you know.
He's middle-aged now.
Nobody actually really knows when he was born, so maybe he's late 40s, early 50s now.
So how's it all going to work out, right?
So effort, continuous effort.
This continued on until 1943.

The war had started, and Executive Order 9066 caused 110,000 Japanese-American citizens and non-citizens alike, infants and grandparents, to be removed to internment camps, surrounded by barbed wire, watchtowers, and armed guards.
Nyogen Senzaki was sent to Heart Mountain, a camp in the desert of Wyoming with 10,000 others.
Perhaps he thought the relocation could be seen as another example of the eastern movement of his teachings.
And he seemed to accept it.
He wrote, "A government must practice its policies without sentiment."
He wrote a poem.
*All Japanese faces will leave California to support their government.
This morning the winding train, like a big black snake, takes us away as far as Wyoming.
The current of Buddhism always runs east.
The policy may support the tendency of the teaching.
Who knows?*
So we can make our own judgments there, right?
Incredibly accepting, compliant.
I guess he knew he couldn't fight it.
But it was a time of great uncertainty.
Before leaving Los Angeles, Senzaki had entrusted his robes to an American student, since he couldn't tell when, if ever, he might return.
But he carried his floating zendo with him and established a sitting place in the small cabin that he shared with a man, a wife, and their small child.
And 10 to 12 people would join him for the same meetings that he'd been carrying on all along.
"These are the happiest and most contented evacuees in the center," he wrote to the 20 or 30 American students with whom he continued to correspond in Los Angeles.
And he managed to send them a lecture every month so they could continue studying.
The young monk, remember the guy in the mountain eating plants, Nakagawa Soan, had planned to visit Senzaki.
They had it all planned to meet in Los Angeles in 1941.
But with the war, that was impossible.
So the two men, who had never met in person, agreed to face each other across the ocean at a certain time on the 25th of every month, Dai Bosatsute, and bow to each other in greeting.
It would take more than a war to keep them apart.
In July 1945, the Supreme Court ruled against the internment of Japanese Americans.
More than 40,000 had already been relocated to places like Colorado, Illinois, and Utah.
And those who returned to the West Coast found the neighborhoods they lived in filled with new immigrants from the South and Mexico.
To anyone who cared to see, it was clear that the Nisei and Isei, first and second and third generations, had demonstrated their loyalty in the war.
And yet their farms had been abandoned, their orchards had died, many of their possessions had been stolen.
The Nichiren Temple in Los Angeles, where more than 600 families had stored their belongings, had been looted and all was lost.
So Senzaki returned to Los Angeles and took up residence again at the homes of various students, once again homeless.
Just as he had been, when Soien Shaku, a teacher, had walked away from him in Golden Gate Park in 1905.
In October 1945, he marked the anniversary of his teacher's death, as he had done every year, with a poem.
*For 40 years I have not seen my teacher, Soien Shaku, in person.
But I have carried his Zen in my empty fist, wandering ever since in this strange land.*
*Being a mere returnee from the evacuation, I could establish Nozando, where his followers could commemorate the 26th anniversary of his death.
The cold rain purifies everything on the earth.
I, in the great city of Los Angeles today, open my fist and spread the fingers at a street corner in the evening rush hour.*
I'm sure they had their grumpy days, but mythic lives are what are left for us.
Soon after his return, he had settled into a small corner apartment on the top floor of the Miyako Hotel in the heart of Little Tokyo.
And it was here, with the sounds of traffic floating up from the streets below, that Senzaki once again set up second-hand chairs acquired from a funeral parlor for the meetings of the postwar Zendo.
On Sundays, a fairly substantial Japanese congregation chanted sutras.
During the week, the English-speaking meeting continued, as they had for the last 25 years.
People meditating in wooden chairs, Senzaki marking off the periods with wooden clappers, reciting the four vows, listening to a short talk, or reading from one of the translations he was working on.
Then tea, along with the Japanese confection, and the meeting would be over.
As before, socializing was discouraged.
If Senzaki found people lingering too long after a meeting, he would punnily suggest it was probably time to go home.
The most important event of these postwar years, as far as Senzaki was concerned, was at last the arrival of Nakagawa Soen in 1949.
The two men who had corresponded for 15 years, and bowed across the ocean to each other every month during the war, at last met face-to-face on San Francisco's Pier 42.
They continued teaching together for a while.
Then in the early 50s, one of Senzaki's most devoted students was a young man, a young American named Robert Aitken.

Like Senzaki, Aitken had spent the war years in internment, in his case on the opposite side, in internment in Japan, where he was introduced to Zen through a chance encounter with a translator and poet named R.
H.
Blyth.
And upon his release, Aitken returned to Hawaii, where he grew up, finished his B.A. in English literature, and wrote a really fantastic senior thesis that became a book about haiku.
You should find it if you don't have it.
Married and spent a semester studying Japanese language and literature in Berkeley, and began seeking a teacher.

In the Christmas vacation of 1947, Aitken and a friend took a trip south to Ojai, where they hoped to find the Indian teacher, you know, who Aitken thought would be about as close as I could get to Zen in this country.
But Krishnamurti was away in India at the time.
So Aitken and his friend continued south.
At Ione Perkins' bookstore in Pasadena, they found Richard Gard working as a chief clerk while working for his doctorate in Buddhist studies at Claremont College.
Gard and Aitken had known each other at the University of Hawaii before the war, and so Gard told Aitken about Nyogen Senzaki.
So Aitken went immediately to the Miyako Hotel in Little Tokyo, and knocked on Senzaki's door.
No internet, right?
Doubtful that there was even a phone in his room.
He found Senzaki alone in his room, and Senzaki showed Aitken a photograph of Nakagawa Soen, and Aitken asked Senzaki if the purpose of zazen was self-realization.
Senzaki says it was.
By the time the visit was over, Senzaki decided that this was what he wanted to do.

So he returned to Southern California, [unclear: "his return for his wife was written by a man, right?"] Return to try to convince his wife, I guess, to move to LA so he could study with Senzaki Roshi, which he did for many years.
And various things happened.
Soen continuing to teach, Soen going back and forth to Japan.
Senzaki only went back to Japan once all these years.
Senzaki encouraging Robert Aitken to go to Japan, which he did, and had various adventures.
And then we'll end our story with the last year of Senzaki's life.
Oh yeah, which is when he returned to Japan.
In 1955, Nyogen Senzaki returned to Japan for the first and last time.
Senzaki visited Soen Shaku's grave at Kamakura, but he stayed mostly at Ryutakuji, a temple, which is like a small temple, avoiding the Rinzai Zen establishment in Kyoto.
As stubborn and independent in Japan as he had been all these years in America.
It had been nearly half a century since Senzaki had left Japan for San Francisco with Soen Shaku.
And though he had grown used to American ways, he never lost his emotional tie to his homeland.
The monks at Ryutakuji were curious about their Roshi's friend from America.
And then various monks met him, who ended up teaching in America, too.
And through Senzaki's close association with Soen Roshi, a number of Americans began to study in Japan: Robert Aitken, Philip Kapleau, Gary Snyder, and a number of others.
But Senzaki was growing old, and he needed an attendant.
Soen asked one of these young monks if he would return to America with Senzaki for about a year.
He was named Tai Shimano, and he ended up being another important teacher in America.
And then in May 1958, a telephone call came during morning zazen.
Soen Roshi left his seat to answer in Japan and did not return.
And after morning zazen, Soen told the monks that Senzaki had died that morning.
They knelt and chanted the four vows together.
Senzaki's last rites, like his life, were conducted his own way.
His body was laid out in a mortuary filled with flowers.
Twelve Japanese priests chanted and placed a memorial tablet on the shrine that had been set up for the occasion.
That much was conventional.
Then someone announced that a talk by Senzaki would be played.
A record table had been set up on a piano, and from it the mourners were quite startled to hear Senzaki's voice, loud and clear.
First in Japanese, quite cheerful, talking and laughing, and then in English.
And then a woman read Senzaki's last words, a statement that he had written in 1936 and revised many times.
And during the reading, Senzaki could be heard correcting the reader's pronunciation.
So he got somebody to read it in English and recorded it.
He clearly knew exactly what he wanted to say.
*I imagine I was going away from this world, leaving all of you behind, and I wrote my last words in English, friends in the Dharma, to be satisfied.*
*I wrote these last words, friends in the Dharma, in English.
Please be satisfied with your own heads.
Do not put any false heads above your own.
Then, minute after minute, watch your step closely.
These are my last words to you.*
He went on, as he said.
He felt he owed some explanation.
*Each head of yours is the noblest thing in the universe.
No god, no Buddha, no sage, no master can reign over it.
Rinzai said, if you master your own situation, wherever you stand is the land of truth.
How many of our fellow beings can prove the truthfulness of these words by their actions?
Keep your head cool and your feet warm.
Do not let sentiments sweep your feet.
A well-trained Zen student should breathe with their feet, not with their lungs.
Breathe with their feet.
This means you should forget your lungs and only be conscious with your feet while breathing.
The head is the sacred part of the body.
Let it do its own work, but do not make any monkey business.
Remember me as a monk.
Nothing else.
I do not belong to any sect or any cathedral.
None of them should send me a promoted priest rank or anything of that sort, like after his death.
I would like to be free from such trash and die happily.*
When people lined up to offer incense, the halls, the side rooms, every stitch of place was filled with people, a student later wrote.
People of all kinds and descriptions, races and creeds.
That to me was really the tribute.
Senzaki's ashes were placed in the Japanese cemetery in East Los Angeles within the site of his stone, so the memorial for the graves of the soldiers of the 442nd Nisei Combat Battalion.
Soen's calligraphy of Senzaki's name was carved into the face of the stone, and on the back, in English, was Senzaki's admonition: Keep your head cool and your feet warm.
Soen Roshi had been present at Senzaki's funeral, and afterward he led two memorial sesshins.

Robert Aitken, who served as his jisha attendant for the first sesshin, where Soen Roshi doubled as the jikijitsu, like the timekeeper and the ino together, Aitken believed this to have been the first time a full seven-day Zen sesshin in America had been conducted in the traditional manner, although it was still somewhat irregular.
Everyone found it very difficult to remember.
Everyone was very unaccustomed to this regime.
It was really hard to not talk and keep our minds centered, and our legs really hurt.
So that, in a way, was Senzaki Roshi's last action, and his death led to the first formal Japanese sesshin we know of in America.
And this is just one of many stories with this kind of flavor.
Incredible patience, great effort and persistence, lots of humility, a little orneriness, a lot of skillfulness.
And I was just thinking and realizing when I first heard this story years ago, I wasn't actually as impressed with it then as I am now.
You know, like, they just sat in chairs and listened to a little lecture.
That was the whole thing.
So as a young proto-monk myself, I was a little dismissive.
But now I get it, I think, a little better.
How amazing that actually was.

That a Japanese Zen priest tossed into this young, you know, some intensive training in his early years, but not near as much training as most of us are going to get, trying to offer this in a way with integrity, a way that would fit, a way that would work.

And a Japanese Zen priest without making any big bones about it, quietly trying to find a way to support himself in a foreign country without good language, just quietly offering zazen, quietly offering teachings, and offering silence, offering the practice of silence.
I never noticed that before either, which is such a powerful part of what we're doing this weekend.
But it's a hard practice.
You have to practice it for a while to appreciate it, and then you realize what a deep and important practice silence is.
But we could never offer the practice of silence, especially in the middle of a busy downtown American town, unless a bunch of us had already really steeped in that, right?
We have a whole community container which makes silence practice possible.
He didn't have any of that.
He just discouraged them from chatting, encouraged a certain kind of settledness, a certain kind of quiet, as befitting and appropriate the practice of Dharma.
And then Nyogen Senzaki's work led directly somehow to his younger monk friend, Soen Roshi, offering this first formal sesshin in America as a memorial.
And in a way, Nyogen Senzaki literally gave his life to create the conditions that allowed this to happen.
So what kind of effort is this?
What is the basis of this kind of long haul effort, long-form effort?
It sure can't just be getting what you want, getting it your way or something.
And it can't be trying too hard and it can't be goofing off either, right?
Somehow he had a steadiness, kept at it week after week.
There was enough money to hire a hall.
There was enough support to have an apartment with enough room, practice there.
So what's the basis of that kind of effort?
Is it vow?
Is the basis a vow?
We don't have recorded that he particularly took a vow, an explicit vow.
The chapter of the book, and this is from Rick Fields' kind of seminal study of Buddhism coming to, you know, convert America, called *How the Swans Came to the Lake*.
The chapter of the book that this is in, Rick Fields calls "Holding the Lotus to the Rock."
Holding the lotus to the rock.
So you've got to be pretty patient.
It's not going to root right away.
Suzuki Roshi in our lineage says our way of practice is to have no gaining ideas.
Just offering something.
Just accepting whatever comes back from the universe.
Being smart for sure, but keeping at it.
So is there a way we can be inspired by these stories to train ourselves, to pay attention ourselves to what our quality of effort is?
Can we have an effort based on gratitude, based on vow?
An effort that's quite a bit softer about results, about getting it the way we want it.
Just making an offering.
And we can always learn about this from the opening to it, from how lovely it feels when our effort is in harmony, when our effort is useful.
And we can learn about this from the opposite too.
Tough lessons for sure, but so important.
When we feel tight.
When we feel upset.
When it's not what we want.
When it's not working.
Can we return to our intention those times?
Can we be interested in the pain, the anger, the tightness?
Can we be grateful for that too, as part of our path?

As we do our best to live out our vow, to be mature beings, to be open beings, devoted to serving and supporting this world, this suffering world, with its shootings, with its growth, with the all of it.
Thank you, Nyogen Senzaki Roshi.
Thank you to all of our ancestors.
Thank you to everybody here.
Let's just continue as best we can.
Thank you for your patience also, with a longer talk.

verbatim.text: Well, good morning everybody. It's wonderful that we get to be together. So many friends, you know, friends from Seattle and Bellingham. Both sanghas, well represented. Well, thanks guy. And friends from further away, Portland, California. Old children of friends, you know, grown up children of friends. So it just goes on, you know. So our theme being effort, I just want to right away appreciate that we're all making an effort to be here.

More friends back there. Lots of other things we could have been doing today. And yet we made an effort to be here. And whether we're staying for the day or the weekend or just the hour, we'll continue to make an effort, right? The effort to be alive. The effort to be ourself. Or try not to be ourself, depending on what's going on.

The effort to help others. The effort to continue. Well, first I think we better acknowledge the difficult events in the world. Another shooting. Horrible. And I realized I almost said, when I was writing this, I almost wrote down senseless shooting. Because it certainly looks senseless from here, doesn't it? An action that we can't really make any sense of.

That a couple would stockpile weapons and make a plan, you know, to kill a bunch of people, coworkers, people on the street, people in a concert hall, people in a synagogue. And probably it's only a matter of time before people in a zendo are shot. It's a matter of time. So it seems so senseless and horrible. But we also know that actually people do things that make sense to them. That seem like the right thing to do in the moment or under the circumstances,

given what they're thinking and feeling. And that's how people are. They were all that way. Subjectively at least, except in some extreme cases, you know, with mental illness, everybody, or maybe we're all somewhat mentally ill anyway, but everybody does what makes sense. So somehow what happened in San Bernardino made sense to that couple. But it doesn't make sense to us.

And maybe this is a blessing that it doesn't make sense to us. It will never make sense to us, we hope. But it's still horrible. So many shootings, the world seems to be coming apart at the seams. It's getting hard to keep track, right? Was the last one Colorado Springs or the other place in Colorado, the theater? Or was it a college in Oregon or was it an elementary school, a post office? What a state of affairs.

And yet here's some interesting other news from the New York Times a little while ago. A survey found that two-thirds of Americans believe that the portion of the world population living in extreme poverty has probably doubled in the last 20 years. So that's 95% of Americans who are completely wrong. In fact, it turns out the proportion of the world's population living in extreme poverty

hasn't doubled, hasn't remained the same in the last 20 years. Actually, it's reduced by half. This article says that the percentage of people has fallen from about 35% of the world's population in 1993 to 14% of the world's population in 2011 living in extreme poverty. So how does this affect the world when 95% of Americans are completely wrong about the way things are going in the world, at least in this particular way?

This is the journalist writing. It was an op-ed piece. And the journalist in it writes. And this also reflects a complete flaw in the way we journalists do our work. We only report on the disasters. In 1990, more than 12 million children died before the age of five. And this toll has dropped by half also. More kids than ever are becoming educated, especially girls. In the 1980s, only half of girls in developing countries completed elementary school.

And now 80% do. So the most important thing going on in the world today is something that we never talk about that we don't believe is happening, a rapid decline in poverty, illiteracy, and disease. Granted that things are still pretty bad, he says. 16,000 children still die unnecessarily every day. He writes, it's maddening in my travels to watch these children dying simply because they were born in the wrong place at the wrong time. But, he says, one reason for our complacency about the world

is the feeling that poverty is inevitable and getting worse. And that is simply not true. That the world's best kept secret, he says, is that we live at a historic moment. A historic inflection point when extreme poverty is retreating rapidly. And the United Nations recently put together a new plan that they hope will lead to essentially the complete elimination of extreme poverty by 2030. The goals are historic, but current evidence suggests that this is actually possible. This can be done.

And there have been recently some other statistics about safety more directly relevant, I guess, to our school shooting horror. That despite the horrible things that are going on in the world that we're aware of, the complete disaster of Syria, you can imagine living in one of those cities in Syria, the rise of ISIS, all these horrible shootings, still on the whole. Much as the world is less impoverished than it ever has been, the world is safer than it ever has been.

Statistics suggest really strongly that this is the safest time in history. You're the least likely to die young from violence or malnutrition or other things that are avoidable. But, you know, it's funny because it's really hard for our mind to think in terms of statistics and probabilities. The concrete is what the mind holds so strongly. And of course, statistics are no comfort to the families of the 14 people who died on Wednesday in San Bernardino.

Just thought they were going to a work party. But I think it's important to see if we can practice holding the horror in this broader concept, this broader reality, that actually there's less suffering, not more, overall, even if there's still far too much. And this doesn't make us complacent, it just spurs us on. It makes us realize what we do really matters, the efforts we make really matter, and we can be part of a solution.

Of course, then, you know, your mind's saying, well, what about global warming? That's another talk. I rode my bike today, anyway. So anyway, I thought we can't really sort of just blithely talk about religion without recognizing the things that are happening, right? So let's return to this theme of effort, which is, I suppose, a kind of effort, the effort to turn towards both the difficult things

and the good things that are happening. So effort's been very much in my mind and in my attention these last weeks because it takes a fair amount of effort to put on these retreats. And I want to especially thank people who did a lot of effort, including everybody in this room, but especially Connie and Kate and Bob Rose and probably other people who I should also name, too. So thank you to all of you wonderful people for all your effort.

It's a lot of work to put on these retreats. And I think even though we're reasonably skillful about how we organize it, of course, there's always room for improvement, and we've done this a lot of times, and written descriptions of things and schedules and plans. Still, it's not so easy because the people who are doing the work for good and ill are people. And people have all kinds of ways of going about effort, don't we?

Sometimes the effort of putting on retreats seems joyful and easy. Other times it seems difficult and burdensome. And it's really hard to tell why that is. Are there particular tasks involved in putting on a retreat particularly difficult? Are some of them easier than others? Is it the task itself? Is it the way we think about the task that makes it easy or difficult? Is it the way we think about the near future?

Like, what's going to happen on Thursday night? Are these people going to arrive? Are we going to be ready? So it's a tricky thing, and the harder we think about it, the crazier we get. And it's not right to just not worry about it either, right? And just like blow it off, oh, it'll work out, you know. They're all nice people. They'll understand, you know, if we're not too organized. So that's not right either. So how do you do it?

And what do we even mean when we say something's hard? Like, what does that actually mean? It has a certain kind of weight in the mind. Is it associated with some mental states? Worry, anger, fear? What does it mean when something's easy? So I was thinking a great advantage of sesshin, of sitting down and being quiet for a while,

is we can watch our mind, you know, watch some of the patterns that are so automatic in us so much of the time when we're running around being busy, and start to discern a little bit, like, well, what is it about effort? What is it in me that supports easeful effort, that supports angry effort, that supports fearful effort? How does it feel in the body? How does it go in the mind? Is the hardness or the difficulty or the ease

baked into the task and the situation? Is it my fault? Is it somebody else's fault? I mean, who knows, you know? I think it's a very complicated and interesting field of study for us and very important to really reflect on what contributes when there's a flavor of suffering in our effort. What is that? The Buddha was quite clear about the root cause of suffering, wasn't he?

Grasping, he said, causes suffering. Aversion causes suffering. There are many different ways, small and large, subtle and blatant, that we want things to be a little different from the way they are. We want ourselves to be a little different from the way we are. And goodness knows, we sure want other people to be a little different from the way they are. And so the Buddha included the idea of right effort

in his eight-fold plan for working on this quality of suffering that we bring to our experience, right effort. And he gave many teachings on that. And then Buddhist practitioners, through the ages, have found ways to practice with this. What's a sustainable effort? And in Bellingham, we've particularly lately been thinking about how did this get here?

How did this happen that we're sitting here in a Soto Zen, Zendo, some of us wearing Tang dynasty Chinese clothing, most of us having grown up in American suburbs? How did this happen? How is this possible? So we've been thinking particularly about the pioneering students and teachers who contributed to establishing this way of practice in America, in North America, in Bellingham, in Seattle, Canada, Mexico. And we've been exploring their stories,

and in our practice period this winter, we're going to particularly explore some of their teachings. And lately I've been thinking about one Zen priest who came to America early on, very early in the 20th century, named Nyogen-Senzaki. And so I want to read you his story, the story of a young Japanese man, Zen Buddhist priest and practitioner who somehow ended up a part of our path,

contributed in some way to this being here today. When I was thinking about the effort of giving a talk, I realized that, yeah, for sure, the suffering involved in giving a talk that happens right before giving a talk usually comes in the form of some kind of worry, right? Your worry, are you going to say the right thing? Is it the right topic? Are you the right person? Do you deserve to be in the seat or whatever?

So I was just curious, what was my worry today? And my worry today is that the talk is going to be way too long. Anyway, I just want you to know that. I don't know if that's true or not because it's just a worry. But there's a little bit to the story of Nyogen-Senzaki, but I think it's worth spending some time on. Nyogen-Senzaki came to America in 1905 with his teacher, So-yen Shaku. And we could do a whole talk on So-yen Shaku.

So-yen Shaku gave a Dharma talk at the World Parliament in religions in the 1880s. As far as we know, the first Japanese or any Asian Zen school teacher to give a talk in America. And 12 years later, he was invited to come back to America. And So-yen Shaku, the teacher of our focus this morning, wrote this poem on the boat. Like this boat on the spring ocean, a monk comes or goes by karma relations. The horizon seems to be extending endlessly. The current, however, takes us to the new world. Yesterday the whales swam around us.

Today the clouds shut off sight of old Japan. Following in the course of Bodhidharma from west to east I go. And turning south I may visit India and Ceylon again making the pilgrimage like Sudana. Before long our boat will enter the Golden Gate. And the seagulls perhaps will guide me to my destination. There's the Japanese priest on the boat in 1905. He was a very innovative guy, So-yen Shaku. Our historian believes he might have been like one of the very, very few Japanese priests interested in the West.

He had also gone and practiced for a while with Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, which was very unusual. So anyway, he was invited back to America by a couple. We had met him when he was there in the 1880s and they had come and visited him in Japan. Mr. Alexander Russell of San Francisco. The Russells had visited So-yen Shaku at his temple in Gakuji during around the world cruise they took. And he had permitted these Americans to join the monks in the training hall. And from these Americans who ate barley gruel with the other monks and sat a full sesshin, So-yen had learned something about how to guide foreigners in Zen.

And so because of this he was happy to accept the invitation from the Russells, which would provide him another opportunity to teach Zen to foreigners. Mr. Russell was a wealthy, civic-minded businessman with interests in mining, rubber, and real estate. And Mrs. Russell had traveled widely in the Orient where, she once told a reporter, she had studied all religions, taking what I think is best from each. The Russells lived on the Great Coast Highway some miles from San Francisco with seven adopted children in the House of Silent Light, as Mrs. Russell called the house, standing on a high bluff overlooking the Pacific surrounded by a wooden fence

that sheltered a traditional Japanese garden from the wind. Entrance was gained through a Japanese-style peat gate. And over the gate the Russells had hung a wood plaque carved with So-yen Shaku's calligraphy of the Chinese characters for silent light. So-yen Shaku's room was specially furnished in Japanese style. This is pretty unusual in 1905, even in California. Mrs. Russell had asked So-yen Shaku to teach her family Zen. And during the nine months that he was their guest, he did just that.

The daily life of this family is very religious, he wrote friends in Japan. Three times a day they practice Zen meditation, sing hymns, ring the handbell, have simple meals to the accompaniment of Western music, and the whole family, even servants, abstains from meat, wine, and smoking. And they practice meditation every day. And Mrs. Russell became the first American to begin Koan studies. That's pretty interesting. The first known Westerner, or at least known American, to do Koan studies in Japanese Zen

was Mrs. Ida Russell of San Francisco in 1905. Most of the Japanese Zen establishment, of course, thought this was impossible for Americans, and completely impossible for women, and therefore completely impossible for American women, to comprehend Japanese Zen. But So-yen Shaku met their objections with a poem, which he addressed to Mrs. Russell, alluding to the famous sixth Patriarch of Chinese Zen. The fifth Patriarch said, told his new monk, Southern monkeys have no Buddha nature.

That monk proved he had Buddha nature by becoming the sixth Patriarch. In any part of the globe, where there is air, fire can burn. Someday my teaching will surely go west, led by you. So-yen Shaku was joined at the Russells by a young student of his, a monk, named Nyogen Sen-saki. Sen-saki's mother had been Japanese, his father Chinese, or Russian, we don't know. He was born and immediately orphaned in Siberia, where a passing Japanese monk found him lying next to his mother's frozen body. He was adopted by a shipwright named Sen-saki,

and then eventually came under care of a Soto Zen priest and Buddhist scholar, who taught him Chinese classics and brought him up. He was a very scholarly young man, supposedly by the time he was 18, he had read the whole sort of Chinese canon of Buddhism, and had studied in Soto Zen and Shingon lineages. And then eventually hooked up with So-yen Shaku, the first teacher in our story. Interestingly, the Japanese are so funny in some ways. Apparently So-yen Shaku never told the Russells who Nyogen Sen-saki was.

He just presented him as like a servant, like the house boy. Didn't say he was an ordained Buddhist priest. And Nyogen Sen-saki lived in the servants' quarters at the Russells, and helped out, you know, humbly helped out. And So-yen Shaku was sent, kind of went home after nine months, and Sen-saki, Sen-saki ended up, oh excuse me, I'm saying the story out of order, So about nine months into their stay, you see I'm already realizing that everybody's just a touch, one moment.

So Sen-saki in the house washed the dishes, did the laundry, cleaned the house, worked hard. But as he remembered, he was a real greenhorn. Although he knew enough English to read Carlisle's Sator Resartus, which I don't know what that is, but it must be hard to read in English. He could read that in his spare time, but he actually couldn't understand the spoken language at all. And finally the housekeeper at the Russells' house decided she'd had enough of him.

So she sent Sen-saki on his way with a five dollar gold piece. So the relationship with this teacher remained obscure to the Americans. And so that evening, So-yen Shaku accompanied Sen-saki on his way to a Japanese hotel in San Francisco. They were walking through the Golden Gate Park when So-yen suddenly stopped, set down Sen-saki's suitcase, which he had been caring for his student, and said,

This may be far better for you. Instead of being hampered by being my attendant monk, just face the great city and see whether it conquers you or you conquered it. Then his teacher turned quickly away, said goodbye, and disappeared into the evening fog. It was the last time Sen-saki ever saw him. So classic Zen story.

Big teaching. Which only would work if you were probably Japanese. You know, we would be like, Wait! Hold on a minute here. So there Sen-saki is. I mean, he was interested in America. Deeply touched by Buddhism, right? Kind of a prodigy young student.

But it said earlier that Nyogen Sen-saki didn't really fit in with the Japanese Zen establishment either, so part of the reason he tagged along probably. In fact, he went off and tried to start a kindergarten because he felt little kids needed to understand something of the practice. And kindergarten was a new idea from Germany he just heard of. But now here he is in America, trying to figure out what to do.

In 1910 Sen-saki began in the hotel business. He started as a porter, worked his way up to clerk, eventually manager. He seemed to have gained this experience though without losing his innocence. And he's not talking to anybody about Buddhism, it says in here too. Just trying to figure out what to do in America. For example, Sen-saki could never understand why some customers would rent a room, stay in it for only a few hours, and then leave. Why was that?

In 1916 he managed to buy a hotel with the help of a business parter. Sen-saki tried but he was not a good businessman. When the hotel lost enough money he gave it up. Like gave it up, you know, here. And became the cook instead. And at the same time he continued teaching Japanese and writing a little bit about Zen in Japanese newspapers. One night in November 1919,

so this is like what, yeah, 14 years since his teacher left, Sen-saki woke from his sleep shivering with cold. He lit a stick of incense and meditated until dawn. Two days later a newspaper arrived from Japan. So-yan Shaku had died at the age of 61 on that day. And from that time he marked So-yan Shaku's death every year. And then in 1922, 17 years after he'd arrived in America, he dared to, quote, utter the B of Buddhism to Americans.

He hired a hall with $20 that he'd saved up from working as a house boy and gave his first lecture. In the lecture he translated a talk that So-yan Shaku had given earlier called First Steps in Meditation. But his English was so heavily accented that he had to write almost all the words down on a blackboard. At the end of the lecture he asked people to leave their names and addresses. From then on he would hire a hall whenever he had enough money.

Sometimes he would simply speak on Buddhism in a friend's parlor. He called these various meeting places his floating zendo. The only image present was a 600-year-old painting of Manjushri, the bodhisattva wisdom whose figure sits on the altar in Zen meditation halls. He had it on loan from an art dealer. In 1927, a brother monk by the name of Mayima visited San Francisco for three days. When he returned to Japan, he helped out by raising $300 for the floating zendo. Within a month, Senzaki had enough money to hire a hall and buy chairs for people to sit on.

He'd now established a zendo, one that he could carry as a silkworm hides himself in his cocoon for 30 more years. In 1931, Senzaki moved his floating zendo to Los Angeles. The money for his move to Turner Street, where he held his meetings, came from the Japanese community. Senzaki kept up the practice he'd started in San Francisco of instructing Japanese on one night and Americans on another. Senzaki had followed Soyanshaka's advice during his years in San Francisco. He had met the challenge of the city head on.

He'd immersed himself in the world, even while he studied and practiced and prepared himself to teach Buddhism. Now in Los Angeles, it was Senzaki the monk that appeared once again. Having nothing in his possession, he has nothing to fear. It was not easy to help Senzaki, since he would give everything away, anything he did not immediately need. A favorite ploy among his students was to leave a $5 bill inside the meditation bell, hoping he wouldn't find it at first. But when Senzaki did find it, he'd immediately invite that person who had left it to join him for dinner in a nearby cafe. Senzaki didn't need much, but he knew how to enjoy himself.

The Zendo in Los Angeles had two names, the Mentor Garden Meditation Hall, mentor garden like kindergarten, and Tozen Zenkutsu, meditation hall for the Eastern Dharma in Japanese. He didn't try to teach his students the traditional cross-legged posture.
